rounds.proof_sketch: Block size is hardcoded to 256 (line 38: const int block_size = 256). Therefore threadIdx.x ∈ [0,255]. Shared memory accesses: (1) shared_mem[tid] where tid ∈ [0,255], (2) reduction loop: shared_mem[tid + stride] where max(tid + stride) = 127 + 128 = 255. All accesses are bounded by index 255. The mutation adds shared_mem[256] which is never read or written.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the shared memory array size from 256 to 257 elements, but this extra element at index 256 is never accessed by any thread. The kernel launches with block_size=256, meaning threadIdx.x is always in range [0,255]. The initial write uses shared_mem[tid] where tid=threadIdx.x. The parallel reduction's maximum access is when tid=127 and stride=128, giving index 255. Since no computation depends on the array size declaration (only on actual indices accessed), and all indices accessed are 0-255 regardless of whether the array is sized 256 or 257, the mutation produces bitwise-identical results for all possible input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation adds an unused shared memory element that is never accessed. No value-level test can trigger a difference because the computational semantics are identical - only indices 0-255 are ever read or written, which are valid in both the original (size 256) and mutated (size 257) arrays. Killing this mutant would require changing the block size to exceed 256, which violates the fixed-configuration contract.
rounds.recommendations: When mutation testing CUDA kernels, mutations to array sizes that exceed the accessed range are semantically equivalent and should be filtered out. A static analysis pass could detect that shared_mem[257] is equivalent to shared_mem[256] when the access pattern is bounded by a smaller constant (blockDim.x=256). Consider adding compile-time assertions like static_assert(BLOCK_SIZE <= SHARED_MEM_SIZE) to document and verify array sizing assumptions.
